name: E-commerce fulfillment warehouse
description: High-SKU e-commerce and omnichannel DCs with dense pick paths, tote and carton flows, and frequent layout tweaks as promotions change. Labor pressure usually concentrates on walking and pick transport rather than heavy pallet-only lanes.
trafficPattern: High pick density, mixed tote/carton moves, dynamic slotting
pageIntro: Fulfillment AMRs help e-commerce warehouses cut walking time when layouts change and pick density is high—not just fixed guided AGV loops. This page ranks vendors whose fleets support AMR transport and pick assist for e-commerce fulfillment, then points you to cost guides and the matcher.

name: 3PL / multi-client warehouse
description: Third-party logistics and shared DCs serving multiple shippers, often with seasonal volume swings, client-specific SOPs, and pressure to pilot automation without locking the whole building into one fixed layout.
trafficPattern: Multi-client zones, seasonal peaks, mixed tote and pallet work
pageIntro: 3PL warehouses need fleets that adapt when clients and volumes change. Shortlist vendors that support AMR, pick-assist, AGV, or pallet workflows for multi-client sites—then run the warehouse matcher with your real volume and layout answers.

name: Manufacturing plant
description: Production and assembly plants moving raw materials, WIP, and finished goods between lines, buffers, and docks. Routes are often more stable than e-commerce pick paths, which favors guided or heavy-payload movers alongside flexible AMRs.
trafficPattern: Line-side delivery, dock-to-buffer, mixed people and forklift traffic
pageIntro: Manufacturing plants often start with pallet movers or AGVs on stable routes, then add AMRs for ad-hoc WIP moves. Compare vendors below, then use the matcher for buy vs lease vs RaaS against your labour and layout inputs.

name: Grocery and cold-chain DC
description: Grocery, foodservice, and cold-chain distribution with temperature zones, food-safety constraints, and dense outbound waves. Automation must respect cold environments, hygiene rules, and tight dock schedules.
trafficPattern: Wave picking, cold-zone moves, tight outbound dock windows
pageIntro: Grocery and cold-chain DCs need vendors that can operate in coolers or adjacent ambient zones and keep wave schedules. Shortlist AMR, AGV, and pallet options here, then confirm temperature ratings and hygiene SOPs with each vendor.

name: Office and retail floors
description: Multi-tenant offices, showrooms, and retail floor plates with hard or mixed surfaces, after-hours cleaning windows, and staff who still handle restrooms and detailing. Robots cover routine vacuum or scrub passes so crews focus on edges and high-touch zones.
trafficPattern: Open aisles after hours, furniture and fixture obstacles, light-to-moderate soil
pageIntro: Office and retail sites usually start with compact autonomous cleaners before industrial scrubbers. Below are vendors that commonly fit this floor plate and soil profile—validate quotes and mapping for your exact layout.

name: Hospital and healthcare floors
description: Hospitals, clinics, and long corridors with infection-control expectations, mixed hard floors, and cleaning windows around clinical schedules. Robots handle routine scrub or vacuum coverage while staff keep restrooms, isolation areas, and detail work.
trafficPattern: Corridor scrubbing, overnight passes, staff and cart traffic
pageIntro: Healthcare sites care about quiet overnight runs, mapped no-go zones, and vendor hygiene documentation. Shortlist scrubbers and office cleaners that fit hospital corridors—confirm clinical SOPs with facilities and infection control before a pilot.

name: Warehouse and distribution floors
description: Warehouse and DC floor cleaning: concrete dust, tracked-in soil, wide aisles, and after-shift or overnight windows. Industrial or large scrubbers usually outperform compact office units on these plates.
trafficPattern: Wide aisles, dock soil, forklift traffic between cleaning windows
pageIntro: Warehouse floors need rugged scrubbers more often than office vacuums. Compare large and industrial cleaning vendors below, then use the cleaning matcher for floor area, frequency, and RaaS vs buy preference.

name: Full-service restaurant
description: Table-service dining rooms with peak-hour runners, busing pressure, and aisle constraints that vary by concept. Robots help with food running or busing when paths are clear and staff still own guest experience and exceptions.
floorAreaBand: Dining room + kitchen paths typical of 80–250 seats
trafficPattern: Peak bursts, server stations, mixed guest and staff traffic
pageIntro: Full-service venues care about aisle width, peak intensity, and guest-facing reliability. These serving-oriented vendors are a starting shortlist—run the restaurant matcher for a fit score based on your seats and layout.

name: QSR and food hall
description: Quick-service restaurants, food courts, and multi-vendor halls with high ticket volume, shared paths, and strong interest in lease or RaaS pilots before buying robots outright.
floorAreaBand: Counter + dining paths typical of high-turnover QSR or food-hall pods
trafficPattern: Dense guest flow, short ticket times, shared corridors
pageIntro: QSR and food halls often pilot serving or bussing robots on lease/RaaS to test congestion and guest reaction. Shortlist vendors here, then confirm aisle width and peak covers in the restaurant matcher.
